questions.subject: ANTHROPOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: examine social stratification using anthropological evidence

stimulus.body: A society ranks occupations and families, with some groups enjoying privileged access to land, education, and political influence.

questions.stem: Which statement about social stratification is best supported by the account?

options.text: Social stratification is the ranking of people and groups into layers with unequal access to valued resources.
Social stratification is the equal distribution of resources among all members of a society.
options.misconception: The unequal access to land, education, and influence shows a ranked social structure.

options.text: Social stratification is a system found only in industrial capitalist societies.
options.misconception: It denies the inequality that the case directly describes.

options.text: Social stratification is the classification of people by age alone.
options.misconception: It wrongly restricts stratification to one kind of society, whereas it is widespread.

questions.explanation: It reduces ranking to age, which is a different kind of differentiation.
questions.hint: Stratification can be based on wealth, rank, power, or ritual status in different societies.

questions.subject: ANTHROPOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: examine social class using anthropological evidence

stimulus.body: Researchers define classes by people's relationship to productive resources and their position in the labor market, and find differing life chances between classes.

questions.stem: The evidence most strongly supports which claim about social class?

options.text: A social class is a group defined entirely by its ritual purity and hereditary occupation.
options.misconception: Class position is defined economically and shapes the opportunities people face.

options.text: A social class is a group defined by its economic position and relationship to the means of production and labor.
A social class is a category of people with identical incomes and identical lifestyles.
options.misconception: It describes caste, which is organized around ritual status rather than economic position.

options.text: A social class is a legal estate established by a constitution.
options.misconception: It imposes an unrealistic standard of complete uniformity within a class.

questions.explanation: It assigns the term to a legal estate, which is a different concept.
questions.hint: Classes are relational categories whose boundaries are often debated and historically changing.

questions.subject: ANTHROPOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: examine caste using anthropological evidence

stimulus.body: A person is born into a hereditary occupational group, marries within it, and is ranked by ritual purity relative to other such groups.

questions.stem: Which choice correctly identifies caste in this case?

options.text: Caste is a social class that anyone can enter or leave through income alone.
options.misconception: Birth, endogamy, hereditary occupation, and ritual ranking together define caste.

options.text: Caste is a temporary association formed for a single ceremonial occasion.
options.misconception: It describes class, which is defined economically rather than ritually.

options.text: Caste is a hereditary, endogamous social group ranked by ritual status and often linked to traditional occupation.
Caste is a political party that competes for elected office.
options.misconception: It reduces caste to a temporary event, whereas it is a durable inherited status.

questions.explanation: It assigns the term to electoral politics, a different kind of organization.
questions.hint: Caste systems vary historically and are not found in every society, but the defining features are hereditary endogamous rank.

questions.subject: ANTHROPOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: examine social status using anthropological evidence

stimulus.body: A teacher is highly respected in one community but has modest income, while a merchant is wealthy but less honored, showing that dimensions of rank can diverge.

questions.subject: ANTHROPOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: examine rank society using anthropological evidence

stimulus.body: A community has ranked positions of prestige with no great differences in wealth, and titles are inherited but do not give their holders control over production.

questions.subject: ANTHROPOLOGY
